title: Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die
gist: A Semiconductor Engineering panel with Teradyne, Advantest, ISE Labs and Keysight says co-packaged optics production test is still mostly single-site, bottlenecked by fiber alignment, connector durability and the cost of testing optical and electrical sides separately. Scaling to volume depends on multi-site probe cards, hardened connectors and design-for-test loopback.

themes.theme: Single-site test and the multi-site path

insights.claim: Most production CPO and optical-engine test solutions today are single-site, with fiber alignment the main bottleneck; multi-site capability would speed the whole industry's ramp.
insights.speaker: Griffin
insights.so_what: Test throughput is a gating factor for CPO volume ramp, favoring vendors that crack multi-site.
insights.quote: Most production solutions today are single-site, and when you talk about the optical engine, the main bottleneck is fiber alignment.
insights.locator: SE: Is it true that you can only test one die at a time today?

insights.claim: For large ASICs such as an 8 kW GPU with connectors on multiple sides, tester power delivery and resource limits make going beyond one die per insertion very hard, whereas single-connector NPO devices must go multi-site to reach high volume.
insights.speaker: Armstrong
insights.so_what: Multi-site scaling will arrive first for NPO-style single-connector parts, not for big-GPU co-packaged modules.
insights.locator: SE: Is it true that you can only test one die at a time today?

insights.claim: Test insertions two and three, which are longer and more complex, are the fertile ground for multi-site, while PIC wafer testing remains single-site with hope from probe card advances, notably Technoprobe.
insights.speaker: Armstrong
insights.so_what: Probe-card suppliers like Technoprobe are a potential enabler and beneficiary of the CPO test ramp.

insights.claim: Armstrong expects more test insertions to be added than removed for now, so the test burden of photonics packages is growing before it shrinks.
insights.speaker: Armstrong
insights.so_what: Rising insertion counts raise test cost per CPO module and favor OSAT/test capacity owners.
insights.quote: I would hope some insertions will go away over time, but right now there are more things being added than being subtracted.
insights.locator: I would hope some insertions will go away

insights.claim: The optical probe or fiber array unit should never contact the device, so repeat testing is near-unlimited in principle; the practical concern is FAU contamination and cleaning, plus occasional FAU crashes in new test bring-up.
insights.speaker: Griffin
insights.so_what: Consumables and cleaning cycles become hidden cost and uptime items in optical test cells.
insights.locator: SE: For these alignment ports, can you repeatedly test at that site?

insights.claim: Device-side optical connectors are designed to be attached once, and every new connector generation changes both the connector recipe and the automation recipe, making connector lifecycle the area needing most effort.
insights.speaker: Griffin
insights.so_what: Connector standard churn delays test automation standardization and raises equipment redevelopment cost.

insights.claim: Test-side connectors must survive tens of thousands to 100,000 insertions versus 20 to 50 for ordinary ones, requiring hardened metal, which risks damaging the softer device-side receptacle before its spec life; device-side robustness will be a key part of winning connector designs.
insights.speaker: Leventhal
insights.so_what: Connector design winners will be those that balance test-side hardness with device-side robustness, an opening for connector suppliers.
insights.quote: It needs to last for tens of thousands or 100,000 insertions.
insights.locator: Matt made a really important point

insights.claim: At wafer and die insertions, simultaneous optical and electrical connection is chiefly an RF probing challenge: modulators and photodetectors are validated via S-parameters, probe cards fit limited RF lines with limited bandwidth, and devices are characterized beyond 200 GHz.
insights.speaker: Yamaguchi
insights.so_what: RF probe-card bandwidth and line count are a technical ceiling on wafer-level photonic test.

insights.claim: Warpage, multi-axis alignment, top versus side access, and a huge BGA pin count compound the difficulty of reliable simultaneous contact.
insights.speaker: Leventhal
insights.so_what: Package warpage in large co-packaged modules directly hurts test yield and fixture design.
insights.locator: Warpage is going to create additional challenges

insights.claim: Optical alignment alone is not hard; the difficulty is designing one scalable test system across the many architecture flavors, with optical and electrical interfaces on top, bottom or two to four package sides across several optical engines.
insights.speaker: Griffin
insights.so_what: Architecture fragmentation raises tester R&D burden and may favor flexible platforms.
insights.quote: So if you look at optical alignment on its own, it’s not that big of a challenge.
insights.locator: At its core, there's an optical and an electrical interface

insights.claim: Bit error rate and AC testing will be among the larger test-time sinks; with good DFT, optical and electrical loopback could run concurrently, whereas today one side is looped back while the other gets a BER test, roughly doubling effective test time.
insights.speaker: Armstrong
insights.so_what: DFT investment in photonic chips could cut test cost materially and is a competitive differentiator.
insights.quote: The more DFT and concurrent testing we do, the better off we’ll be in the long run.
insights.locator: I also chair the IPSR test roadmap for photonics

insights.claim: Most customers going to volume will have electrical, optical or combined loopback, but which approach wins remains undecided.
insights.speaker: Griffin
insights.so_what: Loopback standards are unsettled, so tester vendors face architecture risk.
insights.locator: The automation challenge is still there

insights.claim: By test time, eye quality is the top measurement, followed by receiver sensitivity and bit error rate; insertion loss gets disproportionate attention only because it is run so often, and wavelength sweeps for optical engines also take substantial time.
insights.speaker: Armstrong
insights.so_what: Time-per-test, not frequency, should drive where test-cost optimization is focused.

themes.theme: Reliability, known-good die and root cause

insights.claim: The goal should shift from known good die to known good and reliable die, since escapes are largely integration-induced: FAU coupling loss after attach, resonance drift versus laser tunability, and thermal and packaging effects.
insights.speaker: Yamaguchi
insights.so_what: Yield risk in CPO sits in assembly, raising value of post-assembly and burn-in test.
insights.locator: I also agree, but we need to be mindful

insights.claim: As systems integrate, the key issue is whether data flows correctly in both directions and how to root-cause failures, which requires gathering diagnostic information as early as possible.
insights.speaker: Leventhal
insights.so_what: Early-stage data collection and analytics tie test to yield learning in CPO ramps.
